lessons.title: Making friends
lessons.scenario: Smarty meets Omar and Zara at the café and hears how they became friends.

items.example: I got to know somebody new at school.
items.note: Say 'get to know somebody' when you spend time with a person and learn about them.

items.example: We hang out at the café on Friday.
items.note: Use 'hang out' for spending relaxed free time together with friends.

items.example: I get on well with my cousin.
items.note: Say 'get on well with' someone when you are friendly and enjoy being together.

items.example: We have a lot in common because we both love music.
items.note: Use 'have a lot in common' when two people like the same hobbies or subjects.

items.example: We lost touch after we finished school.
items.note: Say 'lose touch' when you stop speaking or sending messages to an old friend.

items.example: I made friends with Zara in art class.
items.note: Use 'make friends with' someone when you become friends for the first time.

grammar.title: Talking about friendship in the past and present
grammar.explanation: Use the present form (get, hang, make, lose) for habits now, and the past form (got, hung, made, lost) to tell how you met.
examples: I made friends with Leo last year.
We hang out at the park every weekend.

practice.prompt: You become friends with a new student. Which phrase fits?
practice.explanation: Make friends with means to become friends with someone.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: We hang out at the café on Saturday.
practice.answer: We hang out at the café on Saturday.
options: We hang out at the café on Saturday.
We lose touch at the café on Saturday.
We go to school on Saturday.
practice.explanation: Hang out means to spend relaxed time together.

practice.prompt: Match the two halves of each sentence.

pairs.left: We like the same music, so we
I like Sam very much and I
We never text now, so we

practice.explanation: Match each situation to the friendship phrase with the right meaning.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence.
practice.answer: I got to know Omar at the library.
practice.explanation: Got to know is the past form of get to know.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Mia and Ana ___ because they both play tennis.
practice.explanation: When two friends enjoy the same sport, they have a lot in common.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: I get on well with my new friend.
practice.answer: I get on well with my new friend.
practice.explanation: Get on well with means to have a good, friendly relationship.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence about the past.
practice.text: I ___ Ben last year and we became good friends.
practice.explanation: Last year is in the past, so use met.

story.hook: How did Omar and Zara become best friends?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat sitting at a cozy wooden café table with two friendly cat friends, Omar and Zara, drinking tea and smiling.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Hello, Omar and Zara! How did you two meet?

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Zara was only an acquaintance at first, but I got to know her in science class.

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Omar is very cheerful, so I made friends with him quickly.

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: We found out we have a lot in common, like hiking and music.

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: We get on well with each other and we hang out here to chat every week.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I hope you never lose touch!

questions.prompt: Where did Omar get to know Zara?
questions.explanation: Omar says he got to know her in science class.

questions.prompt: Why do Omar and Zara have a lot in common?
questions.explanation: Omar says they have a lot in common, like hiking and music.

mission.setup: You are at the café with Smarty. Tell Smarty about a friend you know.

turns.smarty: How did you make friends with your best friend?
accept: ^i (?:made friends with|got to know|met) (?:him|her|my friend|sam|mia|leo|ana) at (?:school|the park|the cafe|work)$
^we (?:met|got to know each other) at (?:school|the park|the cafe|work)$
turns.example: I made friends with Mia at school.
turns.hint: Say where you met or made friends with your friend.

turns.smarty: That is nice! Do you get on well with your friend?
accept: ^yes i get on well with (?:him|her|my friend)$
^yes we (?:get on well|hang out|have a lot in common)$
turns.example: Yes, I get on well with her.
turns.hint: Say Yes, I get on well with him or her.

exposure.gloss: someone you know a little, not a close friend
happy and smiling
talk in a friendly, relaxed way

lessons.title: Been there
lessons.scenario: Mia and Sam show Smarty travel photos at the café.

items.example: I have been to France and Spain.
items.note: Say 'I have been to' a place when you visited it at some time in your life.

items.example: I have never tried Japanese soup.
items.note: Use 'I have never tried' for a food, sport, or activity you have not done in your life.

items.example: I have visited three countries so far.
items.note: Add 'so far' to mean up to now, with more still possible in the future.

items.example: We have not seen Sam for ages.
items.note: Say 'for ages' when you mean for a very long time.

items.example: I have played tennis once or twice.
items.note: Use 'once or twice' when you have done something only one or two times.

items.example: Have you ever been to Italy?
items.note: Put 'ever' in questions to ask about any time in a person's whole life.

grammar.title: Present perfect for life experiences
grammar.explanation: Use have or has + past participle (been, tried, visited) to talk about experiences in your life without saying the exact date.
examples: I have been to Japan once or twice.
Have you ever tried spicy noodles?

practice.prompt: You visited Germany in the past and came back. Which phrase fits?
practice.explanation: I have been to means you visited a place at some time in your life.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.explanation: Never tried means you have not done it at any time in your life.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning.
practice.explanation: Each expression describes how much or how long up to now.

practice.prompt: Build the question.
practice.answer: Have you ever been to Uzbekistan?
practice.explanation: Use Have you ever been to to ask about a place someone has visited.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: We have read two books ___ this month.
practice.explanation: So far means up to now in this month.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: I have been to Japan once or twice.
practice.answer: I have been to Japan once or twice.
practice.explanation: Once or twice tells how many times you visited.

practice.prompt: Complete the question.
practice.text: ___ tried spicy fish soup?
practice.explanation: Use Have you ever with tried to ask about life experience.

story.hook: Which unusual activity has Sam never tried?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat looking at travel postcards spread on a café table with Mia and Sam.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Look at this keepsake from my trip! I have been to Italy and Spain so far.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Fantastic! Have you ever been to a desert, Sam?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Yes, I have been to a desert once or twice with my uncle.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: I have never tried riding a camel. It looks unusual!

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I have wanted to go back there for ages.

questions.prompt: How many times has Sam been to a desert?
questions.explanation: Sam says he has been to a desert once or twice.

questions.prompt: Which countries has Mia been to so far?
questions.explanation: Mia says she has been to Italy and Spain so far.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you about places you have visited and things you have tried.

turns.smarty: Have you ever been to another country?
accept: ^(?:yes )?i have been to (?:uzbekistan|england|brazil|france|germany|spain|italy|china|japan)(?: once or twice)?$
^no i have never been to (?:uzbekistan|england|brazil|france|germany|spain|italy|china|japan)$
turns.example: I have been to England once or twice.
turns.hint: Say I have been to... and name a country.

turns.smarty: What is something you have never tried?
accept: ^i have never tried (?:sushi|tennis|climbing|spicy soup|japanese food|italian food|french bread)$
^i have never tried (?:tennis|basketball|football|swimming)$
turns.example: I have never tried spicy soup.
turns.hint: Start with I have never tried...

exposure.gloss: a small object you keep to remember a place or person
different from what you normally see
wonderful and very exciting

lessons.title: How long?
lessons.scenario: Ben and Lily tell Smarty how long they have lived in town and played music.

items.example: How long have you known Lily?
items.note: Ask 'How long have you…?' to find out the time from the start until now.

items.example: I have studied English for three years.
items.note: Use 'for' with a number of minutes, days, months, or years to show how long.

items.example: I have played the piano since I was a child.
items.note: Use 'since' with a starting point in the past, like a year, a day, or 'since I was a child'.

items.example: I have lived in this house all my life.
items.note: Say 'all my life' for something that started when you were a baby and is still true.

items.example: Have you visited the museum recently?
items.note: Use 'recently' for something that happened a short time ago.

items.example: I have been very busy at school lately.
items.note: Put 'lately' at the end of a sentence to talk about the past few days or weeks.

grammar.title: for vs. since with the present perfect
grammar.explanation: Use for + a length of time (for three years, for ages). Use since + when it started (since Monday, since I was a child).
examples: We have been friends for three years.
She has lived here since she was a child.

practice.prompt: Which phrase gives a starting point in the past?
practice.explanation: Since shows when an action or state began.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence with the right time phrase.
practice.text: Ben has played the guitar ___.
practice.explanation: Use for with a period of time like three years.

practice.prompt: Match each question or start with the best ending.
practice.explanation: Match the grammar structure and meaning of each time expression.

practice.prompt: Build the question.
practice.answer: How long have you studied music?
practice.explanation: Start with How long have you to ask about duration up to now.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
options: I have painted all my life.
practice.explanation: Recently means a short time ago.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: I have lived here all my life.
practice.answer: I have lived here all my life.
practice.explanation: All my life means from birth until now.

practice.prompt: Smarty has known Ben for a very long time. Which phrase fits?
practice.explanation: For ages means for a very long time.

story.hook: How long has Lily played the violin?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat talking with Ben and Lily outside a sunny café, with Lily holding a violin case.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: How long have you lived in this neighbourhood, Ben?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I have lived here all my life! My family has been here for a decade.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: And what about you, Lily? How long have you played the violin?

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: I have played since I was a child. Music was my childhood dream.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: We have practised together for three years, and we have written a new song recently.

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Yes, we have worked very hard lately!

questions.prompt: How long has Ben lived in the neighbourhood?
questions.explanation: Ben says he has lived there all his life.

questions.prompt: How long have Ben and Lily practised together?
questions.explanation: Ben says they have practised together for three years.

mission.setup: Smarty wants to know how long you have had a hobby or known a friend.

turns.smarty: How long have you studied music?
accept: ^i have studied music for (?:one|two|three|four|five|six|seven|eight|nine|ten) years$
^i have studied music (?:since i was a child|all my life|for ages)$
^for (?:one|two|three|four|five) years$
turns.example: I have studied music for three years.
turns.hint: Answer with for three years or since I was a child.

turns.smarty: Have you tried any new hobby recently?
accept: ^yes i have (?:tried|started) (?:painting|drawing|swimming|tennis|guitar|piano) recently$
^no i have been busy lately$
turns.example: Yes, I have started painting recently.
turns.hint: Use recently or lately in your answer.

exposure.gloss: a period of ten years
the time when you were a child
the part of a town near your home

lessons.title: Review
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Ana review friend phrases and life experiences at the café.

practice.prompt: Ana moved away and stopped calling her old classmate. They ***.
practice.explanation: Lost touch means stopped speaking or writing to a friend.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Smarty has loved fish ___ he was a kitten.
practice.explanation: Use since before a starting point in the past.

practice.prompt: Match the phrases from Lessons 1–3.
practice.explanation: Each beginning pairs naturally with its ending.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence.
practice.answer: I have been to four museums so far.
practice.explanation: So far shows the total up to now.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: We have a lot in common and hang out every Friday.
practice.answer: We have a lot in common and hang out every Friday.
options: We have a lot in common and hang out every Friday.
We lost touch and never hang out.
We have been to France once or twice.
practice.explanation: Have a lot in common and hang out describe close friends.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: We have been best friends for three years.
practice.answer: We have been best friends for three years.
practice.explanation: Use for three years for a period of time.

story.hook: What special day are Ana and Leo celebrating at the café?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat sitting at a café table with Ana and Leo, who have a small cake with a candle.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Have you ever visited this café before, Ana?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Yes, I have been to this café once or twice! Leo is my favourite companion here.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Today is our friendship anniversary! We got to know each other for three years ago, and we have never lost touch.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: We have a lot in common, and we have hung out every weekend since I was a student.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Congratulations! Have a wonderful day!

questions.prompt: Has Ana visited the café before?
questions.explanation: Ana says she has been to this café once or twice.

questions.prompt: How often do Ana and Leo hang out?
questions.explanation: Ana says they have hung out every weekend.

mission.setup: Tell Smarty about a place you have visited and a friend you hang out with.

turns.smarty: Which place have you been to that you really liked?
accept: ^i have been to (?:the park|the museum|the cinema|france|spain|italy|japan|uzbekistan|england)$
^i have been to (?:the sea|the mountains|a forest)$
turns.example: I have been to the museum.
turns.hint: Say I have been to... and name a place.

turns.smarty: How long have you known your friend?
accept: ^i have known (?:him|her|my friend) (?:for three years|for ages|since i was a child|all my life)$
^(?:for three years|for ages|since i was a child)$
turns.example: I have known my friend for ages.
turns.hint: Answer with for ages, for three years, or since I was a child.

exposure.gloss: a friend who spends time or travels with you
a special date you celebrate every year

lessons.title: At the café
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Leo order drinks and snacks at the busy café.

items.example: I would like a hot latte, please.
items.note: A 'latte' is a warm coffee drink made with lots of steamed milk.

image.describe: a warm ceramic cup of latte with foamy milk art on a wooden saucer

items.example: This fresh croissant is delicious for breakfast.
items.note: A 'croissant' is a flaky, curved French pastry often eaten in the morning.

image.describe: a golden flaky crescent-shaped croissant on a small white plate

items.example: Two lattes to take away, please.
items.note: Say 'to take away' when you want to carry your food or drink outside the café.

items.example: Excuse me, is this seat taken?
items.note: Ask 'Is this seat taken?' politely before sitting at an empty chair near someone.

items.example: You paid last time, so it is my round today.
items.note: Say 'My round' when it is your turn to buy drinks for everyone at the table.

items.example: Excuse me, could we have the bill please?
items.note: Say 'the bill please' when you are ready to pay at the end of your visit.

practice.prompt: Look at the picture of a warm drink with foamy milk. Which word fits?
practice.explanation: A latte is a hot drink with lots of warm milk.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: Can I have a croissant to take away?
practice.answer: Can I have a croissant to take away?
options: Can I have a croissant to take away?
Could I have the bill please?
practice.explanation: To take away means you will eat or drink it outside.

practice.prompt: Match each café phrase with when you say it.

pairs.right: When it is your turn to pay for drinks

practice.explanation: These three phrases help you sit, treat friends, and pay in a café.

practice.prompt: Build the polite question.
practice.explanation: Ask Is this seat taken? before sitting down.

practice.prompt: Leo bought the drinks yesterday. Complete what Smarty says.
practice.text: Put your wallet away! It is ___.
practice.explanation: My round means it is your turn to buy the drinks.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: Excuse me, could I have the bill please?
practice.answer: Excuse me, could I have the bill please?
practice.explanation: Polite way to ask to pay at a café.

practice.prompt: You want to order a drink politely. Which words start your sentence?
practice.explanation: Use Can I have a latte, please? to order.

story.hook: Who pays for the lattes and croissants at the café?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat and Leo at a busy café counter with lattes and croissants on a tray.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Look at the menu board! The barista makes great drinks here.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I would like a latte and a warm croissant, please. Sit here, or to take away?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Let us sit here. My round! I will pay for both of us.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Thank you! Look, there is a table by the window. Excuse me, is this seat taken?

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: No, sit down! Enjoy your pastry!

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: That was delicious. Excuse me, the bill please!

questions.prompt: What does Smarty order at the café?
questions.explanation: Smarty orders a latte and a warm croissant.

questions.prompt: What does Smarty ask Mia before sitting down?
questions.explanation: Smarty asks Mia: Is this seat taken?

mission.setup: You are ordering with Smarty at the café.

turns.smarty: I am ordering now. What would you like from the café?
accept: ^(?:can i have|i would like) a (?:latte|croissant)(?: to take away)?(?: please)?$
^a (?:latte|croissant)(?: and a (?:latte|croissant))?(?: please)?$
turns.example: Can I have a latte, please?
turns.hint: Ask for a latte or a croissant.

turns.smarty: We are finished! How do we ask to pay?
accept: ^(?:excuse me )?(?:could i have |can i have )?the bill please$
^my round$
turns.example: Excuse me, the bill please.
turns.hint: Say The bill please or My round.

exposure.gloss: a big board on the wall showing food and prices
a person who makes coffee drinks in a café
a baked sweet or savoury snack like a croissant

lessons.title: Catching up
lessons.scenario: Zara and Tom bump into each other at the café after a long time.

items.text: What have you been up to?
forms: What has he been up to?
What has she been up to?
items.example: Hi Tom! What have you been up to?
items.note: Ask 'What have you been up to?' when you meet a friend and want to hear their recent news.

items.example: Guess what! I won first prize!
items.note: Say 'Guess what!' right before you share exciting or surprising news.

items.example: I have just heard that Mia got a new job.
items.note: Use 'I have just heard' to tell someone news you learned a moment ago.

items.example: You will never believe who I saw at the station!
items.note: Say 'You will never believe…' before telling a very surprising story.

items.example: Hello Zara, long time no see!
items.note: Say 'long time no see' when you meet a friend you have not seen for weeks or months.

items.example: Sit down and have a tea. Any news?
items.note: Ask 'Any news?' as a quick, friendly way to ask what is new in someone's life.

practice.prompt: You see an old friend after six months. What do you say?
practice.explanation: Long time no see is a friendly greeting after a long time apart.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: What have you been up to lately?
practice.answer: What have you been up to lately?
options: What have you been up to lately?
practice.explanation: What have you been up to? asks about recent activities and news.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its purpose.

pairs.right: Telling news you learned moments ago

practice.explanation: Each phrase introduces or asks for news in conversation.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence.
practice.explanation: You will never believe introduces a big surprise.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ that Omar passed his driving test!
practice.explanation: Use I have just heard to share fresh news.

practice.prompt: Say the greeting aloud.
practice.text: Long time no see! Any news?
practice.answer: Long time no see! Any news?
practice.explanation: Natural way to greet a friend and ask for updates.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence about something that happened moments ago.
practice.text: ___ arrived at the café!
practice.explanation: Use I have just for an action finished a moment ago.

tell news clearly to a group of people
surprise someone very much

lessons.title: Personality
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia describe their friends' personalities over tea.

items.example: Leo was shy at first, but now he loves to sing.
items.note: Someone who is 'shy' feels quiet or nervous when meeting new people.

image.describe: a cute small cat peeking shyly from behind a big menu card at a café table

items.example: Ana is generous and always shares her snacks.
items.note: A 'generous' person likes to give time, help, or presents to others.

items.example: Sam is reliable and always arrives on time.
items.note: Someone who is 'reliable' does what they promise and can be trusted.

items.example: My brother is stubborn and never changes his mind.
items.note: A 'stubborn' person refuses to change their plan or idea even when others ask.

items.example: Zara is easy-going and never gets angry.
items.note: Someone who is 'easy-going' is relaxed and happy with almost any plan.

items.example: Smarty has a great sense of humour and makes us laugh.
items.note: Someone with a good 'sense of humour' enjoys jokes and makes other people smile.

practice.prompt: Look at the picture of the cat hiding behind the menu. Which word fits?
practice.explanation: Shy describes someone who feels nervous or quiet around new people.

practice.prompt: Match each personality word with its meaning.
practice.explanation: Each word describes a different kind of character.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Ben is very ___ and never worries about small problems.
practice.explanation: Easy-going means relaxed and calm.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence.
practice.answer: Mia has a great sense of humour.
practice.explanation: Have a sense of humour means to enjoy funny things.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.explanation: Reliable means you can depend on that friend.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: My best friend is generous and easy-going.
practice.answer: My best friend is generous and easy-going.
practice.explanation: Generous and easy-going are positive character words.

practice.prompt: Because Leo is easy-going, everyone ___ him.
practice.explanation: Easy-going people are easy to get on well with.

lines.speaker: Smarty

questions.prompt: How is Omar when you first meet him?

questions.prompt: What is Omar stubborn about?
questions.explanation: Mia says he can be stubborn about his favourite football team.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you to describe a friend or family member.

turns.smarty: Tell me about your best friend. What is he or she like?
accept: ^(?:he|she|my friend) is (?:generous|reliable|easy going|shy)(?: and (?:generous|reliable|easy going))?$
^(?:he|she) has a (?:good |great )?sense of humour$

accept: ^yes (?:he|she) has a (?:good |great )?sense of humour$
^yes (?:he|she) is very funny$

exposure.gloss: making good, careful decisions
having good manners and speaking kindly
liking to talk a lot

lessons.title: Review
lessons.scenario: Smarty, Leo, and Zara catch up and order at the café.

practice.prompt: Which item is a flaky breakfast pastry?
